cita: Ward (2025). MemoriesDB: A Temporal-Semantic-Relational Database for Long-Term Agent Memory.
problema: Long-running LLM agents suffer 'context decoherence': facts and intentions drift out of scope as sliding-window/RAG/episodic-cache techniques accumulate history, losing the temporal-causal thread that ties past experience together.
mecanismo: Each memory is a vertex (timestamp, kind, multi-view normalized embeddings, metadata) linked by directed, labeled, weighted/confidence-scored edges (Sec.2.1-2.2) on top of Postgres+pgvector, append-only; a coherence metric C = e^-d(Mi,Mj) (Eq.5, Sec.2.4) measures semantic drift between memories as a staleness proxy; multiple agents share one instance via namespaces + cross-agent edges (Sec.3.1), and background maintenance (normalization, metadata pruning, edge cleanup, Sec.4.4) performs consolidation.
evaluacion: The paper explicitly states it reports NO formal benchmark: 'the performance figures in this section are illustrative estimates ... not results from formal benchmarking' (Sec.4, before Table 1) and 'no formal metrics are yet reported' (Sec.4.6) -- qualitative description of a single-author prototype only.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The coherence metric C=e^-d(Mi,Mj) (Eq.5) is a plausible staleness-detection primitive, but the paper admits it has no empirical validation of its drift-mitigation claim (Sec.4).
Background pruning/normalization (Sec.4.4) resembles MF's gotcha-to-recipe promotion idea in spirit, but is described only qualitatively, with no measured effect.

notes: RECONSIDERAR: single-author prototype, self-declared 'illustrative estimates ... not results from formal benchmarking' (Sec.4) and 'no formal metrics are yet reported' (Sec.4.6) -- same weak-evidence flag as the extraction pass; digested per convention, inclusion decision remains human.

cita: Bae et al. (2022). Keep Me Updated! Memory Management in Long-term Conversations.
problema: Long-term conversational memory accumulates without update: once a fact is stored (e.g. 'sore throat'), prior long-term-dialogue systems never revise or remove it even after it becomes outdated, causing 'Pink Elephant Paradox' confusion when the bot references stale information in later sessions.
mecanismo: At the end of each session, memory is stored as unstructured natural-language sentences (not slots/graphs); a fine-tuned T5 classifier scores every (old-memory, new-summary-sentence) pair with one of four pairwise operations -- PASS/REPLACE/APPEND/DELETE (Algorithm 1, Sec.4.3) -- so DELETE can retire BOTH sentences once a state no longer applies ('forgetting a completed state'); retrieval uses a dual-encoder BERT (CPM) with triplet loss, top-k at inference (Sec.4.1/Appendix B.3).
evaluacion: Evaluated on CareCallmem, a multi-session extension of the Korean CareCall dataset (5 sessions/episode); compares memory-update (the proposed 4-op mechanism) against memory-accumulate (never revising) via F1/BLEU on generated responses, with a separate operation-classifier ablation over encoder variants (Table 3).
numeros_clave: Table 3: NLI-transfer fine-tuned classifier reaches 88.69% set-level F1 for operation prediction (best variant); Table 4: memory-update beats memory-accumulate on F1/BLEU, with the largest gap in later sessions and in the 22.4%-of-turns 'memory turns' subset that explicitly use memory.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: This is THE canonical staleness paper: Table 4 measures that explicit update/delete of outdated memory beats pure accumulation, directly confirming MF's need for staleness-aware writes rather than append-only logs.
The 4-op PASS/REPLACE/APPEND/DELETE classifier (Algorithm 1) is a concrete, learnable consolidation policy MF could adapt for deciding when a doc/gotcha supersedes a prior one.

notes: Algorithm 1/Sec.4.3 (4-op classifier); Table 3 (classifier F1); Table 4 (update vs accumulate).

cita: Li et al. (2025). Hello Again! LLM-powered Personalized Agent for Long-term Dialogue.
problema: Long-term dialogue agents need both persistent event memory across sessions AND consistent, evolving personas for user and agent, but prior work addresses these separately (event-memory-only or persona-only systems), hindering long-term consistency, and pure semantic-similarity retrieval surfaces irrelevant memories.
mecanismo: LD-Agent keeps a long-term memory bank (event summaries as embeddings via MiniLM encoder, Sec.3.2.1) plus a short-term cache of the ongoing session (with timestamps, Sec.3.2.2), consolidated into the long-term bank once the cache's idle interval exceeds beta=600s (Eq.3, an event-driven consolidation trigger); retrieval combines topic-overlap + time-decay + a semantic threshold gamma=0.5, returning 'No relevant memory' rather than a weak forced match (Sec.3.2.1, Eq.1-2); a separate dynamic persona bank tracks both user and agent traits (Sec.3.3).
evaluacion: Evaluated on MSC and Conversation Chronicles (CC) for effectiveness, plus cross-domain transfer (train on one, test on the other) and Ubuntu IRC (multiparty) for generality; an ablation (Table 2, Sec.4.4) isolates each module's contribution to BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR.
numeros_clave: Table 2 ablation: the event-memory module contributes the most to BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR over a ChatGLM-tuned backbone on MSC (Sec.4.4); cross-domain transfer to CC and multiparty transfer to Ubuntu IRC (RQ2) both hold up without in-domain retraining.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Returning an explicit 'No relevant memory' signal below threshold gamma=0.5 (Eq.1-2) rather than forcing a weak retrieval match is measured evidence for MF's preference for abstaining over hallucinated-relevance retrieval.

The 600s-idle-interval deterministic trigger (Eq.3) that flushes short-term cache into long-term memory is a concrete, cheap consolidation-trigger pattern MF could mirror for session-to-durable-doc promotion.

notes: Sec.3.2.1-3.2.2 (dual memory + consolidation trigger); Table 2 (Sec.4.4 ablation).

cita: Putta et al. (2026). Self-Reflective Memory Consolidation in Agentic Architectures. International Journal of Computer Applications, 187(73).
problema: The paper frames long-context agentic reasoning as suffering memory drift and representational decay across repeated updates, motivating a reflection-based consolidation loop to keep stored/retrieved representations aligned.
mecanismo: SRMA (Self-Reflective Memory Architecture) combines episodic encoding, a reflection-scoring step, adaptive retrieval, and an energy-based correction term into one consolidation cycle (Sec.3); updates compare stored vs retrieved states and apply a controlled adjustment rather than static overwrite, reporting retention-alignment (rho), reflective-drift (Psi), and reflective-efficiency (Omega) metrics.
evaluacion: Evaluated (per the paper) on MemoryBank, LME (LongMemEval), and DuLeMon, comparing SRMA against these DATASET names as if they were baseline METHODS (Table 2) -- a red flag noted below; an ablation (Table 9, Sec.5.6) removes reflection-scoring / energy-regularization / feedback-correction individually and jointly.
numeros_clave: As reported (unverified against real baselines, see notes): rho=0.91, Psi=0.048, Omega=0.89 (vs baselines ~0.82-0.84, Table 2); 0.38s per update on an RTX A6000 (Sec.3.5, no baseline cost comparison given); Table 9 ablation shows retention (rho) drops and drift (Psi) rises when reflective modules are removed.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The reflection+energy-regularization consolidation loop (Eq.9) is architecturally plausible for MF's promotion-of-transient-gotchas idea, but the paper's own comparison table (Table 2) appears to pit SRMA against the CITATIONS for the MemoryBank/LME/DuLeMon DATASETS rather than real competing methods, so the magnitude of improvement is not trustworthy evidence either way.

notes: RECONSIDERAR: low-apparent-rigor venue (International Journal of Computer Applications), templated-looking prose (repeated 'Early/Mid/Late-phase' phrasing per equation, Sec.3.1-3.4), Table 2 (Sec.5.1) compares 'Ours' against rows [42]/[13]/[19] which are the dataset citations for MemoryBank/LME/DuLeMon, not baseline methods, and the proposed SRMA (encoder+recurrent attention over embeddings, Sec.3) never integrates an LLM despite the 'agentic architectures' title -- same flag as the extraction pass, decision left human.

cita: Ke et al. (2025). Flexibly Utilize Memory for Long-Term Conversation via a Fragment-then-Compose Framework.
problema: Summarizing conversation history into memory compresses and mixes redundant/irrelevant information together, making it hard to selectively combine just the key facts that are scattered across different sessions when retrieving memory for a new query.
mecanismo: FraCom's Fragment step prompts an LLM to extract propositions (predicate+arguments) per utterance, inspired by propositional representation in Cognitive Psychology (Sec.3.1); the Compose step incrementally builds a propositional graph where nodes are propositions/predicates/arguments connected by SHARED arguments across sessions (Algorithm 1/Sec.3.2); retrieval is 'plausible retrieval' -- cosine similarity over Sentence-BERT embeddings of arguments plus a threshold theta (Sec.3.3) -- surfacing exact AND plausibly-related propositions instead of whole summaries.
evaluacion: Evaluated across 3 LLM backbones x 4 datasets (Conversation Chronicles, MSC, GC, LongMemEval) against summary-based baselines (Context/Rsum/MemoChat/MemoryBank/COMEDY) on BLEU-4/ROUGE-L/BertScore, plus custom Memory-Usage/Memory-Capacity/M1 metrics (Appendix D) and an ablation removing plausible-retrieval (Table 3).
numeros_clave: Table 3 ablation: removing plausible-retrieval measurably degrades M1-score and BLEU/ROUGE/BertScore on CC/LongMemEval (averaged across LLMs); Table 1: FraCom leads BLEU-4/ROUGE-L/BertScore in most of the 3-LLM x 4-dataset combinations vs the 5 baselines.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The propositional graph (predicate+arguments as nodes, Sec.3.2) is a derived index over raw conversation -- a concrete alternative shape (fine-grained fragments vs whole-document chunks) for MF's Tier-3 derived-index-as-cache layer.
Table 3's ablation isolates plausible-retrieval's measured contribution (vs exact-match retrieval alone), directly confirming that measured, tunable retrieval strategy matters for MF's own layer.

cita: Maharana et al. (2024). Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents.
problema: No benchmark existed to evaluate LLM agents' memory over VERY long conversations (existing eval spans <=5 sessions, ~1K tokens); it's unknown whether RAG/long-context LLMs actually understand causal/temporal structure across dozens of sessions rather than just superficial recall.
mecanismo: Not a memory mechanism itself -- LoCoMo is an evaluation benchmark/dataset: a machine-human pipeline generates very-long dialogues (LLM agents with personas + temporal event graphs + reflect-and-respond, up to 32 sessions/~600 turns/~16K tokens, human-verified) and evaluates 3 tasks (QA across 5 reasoning types, event-graph summarization via FactScore, multimodal dialogue generation) against Base-LLM / long-context-LLM / RAG (DRAGON retriever) methods under test.
evaluacion: Evaluates existing memory approaches (not a new mechanism of its own) on the LoCoMo benchmark: QA (single-hop/multi-hop/temporal/open-domain/adversarial, partial F1), event-summarization (FactScore F1 vs the ground-truth event graph), and multimodal dialogue generation (MMRelevance).
numeros_clave: RAG improves 12-20pp over base-LLM on QA but still lags human performance by 36pp (QA) / 41pp (temporal reasoning); long-context LLMs drop -65% vs base on adversarial questions (Sec.1/Sec.5); LoCoMo averages 16x the conversation length of MSC (Table 1).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Measured retrieval precision for RAG methods against a very-long-conversation ground truth (Sec.4/Sec.5) is exactly the kind of measured-retrieval evidence MF's G-M2 anchor is looking for, showing RAG helps but plateaus well below human recall.

The 65% adversarial-question drop for long-context-LLM-only approaches is indirect evidence against 'just use a bigger context window instead of memory', relevant context for MF's cost/architecture tradeoff even though the paper doesn't measure token cost directly.

notes: Sec.1/Sec.5 (headline RAG-vs-human gaps); Table 1 (dataset scale comparison).
